narrative:
The model estimates you have a 17% chance of failing your final year. While this is not a high probability, it is enough for the school to require you to take remedial courses as a precaution.

The prediction that you might fail is driven mainly by three aspects of your situation. The most influential factor is that you have had no past class failures. Surprisingly, this actually pushes the model toward expecting you to fail. Among students who passed, zero past failures is the average, yet in your specific combination of circumstances the model sees this clean record as a signal that you may not have developed the resilience or study habits needed for final-year demands. 

The second strongest influence is your father’s higher education level. This works in your favor and pulls the prediction toward passing, because students whose fathers completed higher education tend to do better. However, this positive effect is not strong enough to outweigh the other signals.

Third, your clear desire to pursue higher education also encourages the model to predict success. Almost every student who passed shares this ambition, so the model sees it as a protective factor, yet again the positive push is smaller than the first influence.

Because the overall risk remains above the school’s safety threshold, remedial courses are mandatory. To improve, you should focus on building consistent study routines now, even though you have no previous failures. Use your strong family support, your wish to continue studying, and your very good health and low absences to create daily habits that turn your ambition into steady progress. Small, regular effort this term can comfortably move you into the passing group.
